background: During 2025, the threat-intelligence firm Synthient aggregated 2 billion unique email addresses disclosed in credential-stuffing lists found across multiple malicious internet sources . Comprised of email addresses and passwords from previous data breaches, these lists are used by attackers to compromise other, unrelated accounts of victims who have reused their passwords. The data also included 1.3 billion unique passwords, which are now searchable in Pwned Passwords.
Working to turn breached data into awareness, Synthient partnered with HIBP to help victims of cybercrime understand their exposure.
how: The published account does not explain the exact way the data was obtained.
outcome: 1,957,476,021 accounts are listed in this breach. This is a count of accounts, not necessarily individual people.
The reported exposed data includes Email addresses, Passwords.
editorial: This entry is not a company being breached. It is an aggregate, two billion addresses collected from credential-stuffing lists that were already circulating, built from other people's breaches and from information-stealing malware on victims' own machines. Nobody was attacked to create it. Which means finding yourself here answers a different question than usual. It does not tell you which service failed.

It tells you that a password of yours, from somewhere, at some point, is in the pool that gets tried automatically against banks, mailboxes and retailers. That is worse in one specific way: there is no single site to go and fix. The part people miss is the stealer-log component.

Credentials harvested by malware come from a compromised device, not a compromised website, so they can include passwords that were never leaked by any company, typed into sites that have never been breached at all. If that is the source, changing one password is not enough; the machine that captured it needs to be cleaned first, or the replacement joins the same list. The useful response is boringly structural.

Unique passwords everywhere, generated and stored in a manager, and two-factor authentication on anything that can reset something else. Aggregates like this one are the reason credential stuffing works at all, and they are the reason it stops working against people who never reuse.

fields.name: Passwords
fields.why: Anyone reusing this password elsewhere has those accounts exposed too, credential stuffing is automated and tries them all within days.

fields.name: Email addresses
fields.why: The address becomes a confirmed, active target, expect more phishing, better aimed.

actions: Change this password anywhere you reused it, starting with your email account, that is the one that can reset all the others.
Expect better-aimed phishing. A message that already knows your name and where you have an account is the whole point of a breach like this.
